name: SLU-PP-332
class: Pan-ERR agonist (small molecule, not a peptide)
evidenceNote: Every published result for SLU-PP-332 comes from cells and mice, nearly all from the lab that created it. No human trial has been registered or reported, so its effects, dose, and safety in people are unknown.
summary: SLU-PP-332 is a lab compound that switches on ERR receptors and mimics parts of endurance exercise in mice. It has never been tested in humans.
keyTakeaway: SLU-PP-332 is a small synthetic molecule, not a peptide, designed at Saint Louis University to activate the estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) that drive muscle's response to aerobic exercise. In mice it raised endurance, energy expenditure, and fat burning, reduced fat mass in obese animals, and protected the heart in a heart failure model. No study in humans has been published or registered. It is not FDA-approved for any use, and athletes are covered by WADA's ban on unapproved substances. Products sold online as a "peptide" are unregulated research chemicals.

blocks.text: SLU-PP-332 is an experimental compound made by chemists and pharmacologists at Saint Louis University, which gives it the SLU in its name. It is a small molecule built around a naphthalene ring system, not a chain of amino acids, even though it is often sold alongside peptides [1][5]. The team first described it in 2023 as a pan-agonist of the estrogen-related receptors, meaning it switches on all three members of that receptor family [1].

It drew attention as a possible "exercise mimetic", a drug that would trigger some of the body's responses to training without the training. Several of its inventors hold shares in Myonid Therapeutics, a company developing medicines aimed at these receptors [1]. The group has since reported a second, chemically different compound, SLU-PP-915, which can be absorbed when swallowed [4].

Estrogen-related receptors (ERRα, ERRβ, and ERRγ) are proteins inside the cell nucleus that turn on genes. Despite the name, they do not respond to estrogen. They control genes for building mitochondria, burning fatty acids, and running the chemical cycles that produce energy, and muscle needs them to adapt to aerobic exercise [4]. Making drugs that activate ERRα had proved difficult, and SLU-PP-332 was reported as the first useful tool that reaches all three, with its strongest effect on ERRα [1].

In muscle cells it increased mitochondrial activity and oxygen use. In mice it shifted muscle toward type IIa fibers, which rely more on oxygen and resist fatigue, and switched on a set of genes normally seen after a bout of aerobic exercise [1]. The authors reported that activation of ERRα in particular was needed for the endurance gain [1]. The compound is not absorbed well by mouth, so in the later comparison study it was given by injection into the abdomen [4].

No. SLU-PP-332 is not approved by the FDA or by any other regulator for any use. A search of ClinicalTrials.gov finds no registered study of it in people [8]. A 2026 systematic review of the ERR agonists reached the same point: all the evidence is from animals and cells, and clinical trials are needed before anything can be said about humans [6].

For athletes, the World Anti-Doping Agency bans at all times any drug with no approval from a health regulator for human use, under its S0 class [7]. Its separate list of banned metabolic modulators already includes related exercise mimetics such as AICAR and GW1516 [7]. Anti-doping scientists have begun mapping how human liver enzymes break SLU-PP-332 down, so that tests can detect its use [5].
The published work is small in volume and comes almost entirely from one research network. All of it is preclinical.

rows: More oxidative muscle fibers and longer running endurance, dependent on ERRα [1]

blocks.text: The obesity study used mice fed a high-fat diet and a genetic strain that overeats. In both, the compound behaved like training: it raised whole-body energy use and fatty acid oxidation and reduced the build-up of fat [2]. In the heart failure study, it activated a broad set of fat-burning and mitochondrial genes in heart muscle and largely normalized the heart's chemical profile, without changing how thick the heart wall grew [3].

What has not been studied matters as much. There are no human data on dose, blood levels, half-life, or side effects. ERRs act in many tissues. The 2026 review found no evident toxicity in the animal work, but those experiments were built to test benefit, not to serve as formal safety testing [6]. Mouse endurance and weight results often fail to carry over to people, which is why the authors themselves describe the compound as a chemical tool rather than a medicine [4].

Vials and capsules labeled SLU-PP-332 are sold online as "research use only" and marketed with the nickname "exercise in a pill." These are unregulated chemicals with no FDA review of what they contain, how pure they are, or whether injectable versions are sterile. Because the compound was shown to work poorly by mouth in mice, capsule products raise a further question about whether they would do anything at all [4]. No human study supports any dose that sellers suggest [6][8].
